detail:

Amazon (AMZN) disclosed an $80 billion secured loan facility that pledges data center equipment as collateral, departing from its usual cash and bond funding.

AWS revenue grew 39% to $46 billion with a $578 billion backlog, giving Amazon the demand signal to justify its aggressive capital spending.

Amazon's total contractual commitments hit $884 billion at September 30, more than doubling year-over-year, with $160 billion locked in for property and equipment.

Recently, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) disclosed a secured loan facility of up to approximately $80.0 billion in its third-quarter 10-Q, filed October 30, 2026. Amazon has mostly paid for its expansion with cash and plain corporate bonds, so offering the equipment itself as security is a new step.

David Ryder / Getty Images

The shares fell 1.41% to $240.35 on October 30 and traded at $240.83 after hours at 7:54 p.m. ET. Tech stocks sold off broadly that day, so the drop can't be attributed to the facility.

AMZN Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

AWS demand looks strong enough to justify the spending. But the cash bill is now bigger than what the business brings in, and Amazon is using financing tools it used to leave to rivals.

What Amazon's $80 Billion Facility Actually Covers

The facility allows "borrowings at our discretion, from Q1 2027 through Q3 2028," at variable interest rates, according to the filing. Amazon has set up the ability to borrow, but it hasn't drawn anything yet and can't until 2027.

Each borrowing comes due five years after it is drawn. Amazon "will grant a security interest in certain purchased assets," which means lenders get a claim on some of the equipment if Amazon doesn't repay.

Amazon.com just dropped Q3 2026 numbers that show a bruising hit to profit even as the business kept pulling in more sales. Net income landed at US$20.7b on revenue of US$201.9b, and earnings per share stepped down sharply from the unusually strong prior quarter.

The stock told a different story. Shares came into today already under pressure over the past three months and slipped another 1.4% in the latest session. That move appears driven more by emotion around the profit reset than by a calm read of the broader earnings picture, which reflected record operating margins.

Love Amazon.com's record operating margins but uneasy about the profit reset and recent share slide? Compare that mix of strength and pressure with our list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals stocks (25 results)

Q3 2026 Earnings Summary

Revenue (Q3 2026 vs. Q3 2025): US$201.9b vs. US$180.2b (up about 12%).

Net Income (Q3 2026 vs. Q3 2025): US$20.7b vs. US$21.2b (slightly lower).

Basic EPS (Q3 2026 vs. Q3 2025): US$1.92 vs. US$1.98 (down about 3%).

Operating Margin (Q3 2026): 13.9%, with record operating profit levels reported for Amazon.com in the quarter.

Amazon is pouring unprecedented cash into AI-heavy infrastructure. Ask Charlie what makes Amazon's AI bet worth $220B in CapEx.

NasdaqGS:AMZN Trailing 12-Month Revenue & Expenses Breakdown as at Oct 2026
Amazon AI thesis: early proof, heavy cost

Supporters argue the Amazon.com AI and cloud build can turn massive spend into durable, high margin engines.

"Rapid advances and adoption of generative AI, coupled with Amazon's deep vertical integration in custom silicon, proprietary models and agent tooling, are now supported by more than US$225b in Trainium revenue commitments and a chips business at over US$25b run rate, which can extend AWS high margin revenue and operating income growth."

Q3 shows real traction. AWS revenue reached US$46b with 38.7% margin and triple digit AI growth, and backlog is US$578b. The catch is that free cash flow over the last year remained deeply negative as the capex bill arrived ahead of those commitments fully converting to cash.

Amazon capex risk: contracts help, cash lags

Skeptics worry the spending cycle turns into a drag if long term deals fail to keep pace with the bill.

"The main thing that has to go right is that Amazon.com turns its very large AI focused CapEx program, including data centers, servers and satellite infrastructure, into long duration contracts that sustain strong free cash flow and attractive returns on invested capital."

The current picture is mixed. On one side, backlog of US$578b and multi year Leo and power agreements support the idea of contracted demand. On the other side, roughly US$220b of 2026 capex and a US$42.4b free cash flow shortfall show the cash strain is already material, and the share price has fallen about 11% over 90 days.

The Nasdaq-100 spent part of Friday, October 30, 2026, below the line that defines a correction, then climbed back above it before the close. It fell 3.46% to close at 28,384.85, after reaching an intraday low of 28,093.24.

Who is Danny / Shutterstock.com

That low sat 10.0% below the October 6 record close of 31,224.47. A correction means a 10% drop from a record, so the index crossed that line during the session. It closed 9.1% below the record, which means it never finished a day in correction.

Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) closed at $690.49, down 3.47%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its lowest close since July 31.

The selling started in chips. Shares of Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) fell 28.6% after it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $16.5 billion it had just reported. Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said, "We're moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the 'show me' phase."

Why the Close Matters More Than the Intraday Low

The correction label is based on closing prices, and buyers came in before the close and raised the index back above the line. Volatility followed the same path. The VIX, which measures how much investors expect the S&P 500 to swing, hit 23.93 during the session but closed at 19.41, up 12.91%.

title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy makes a strong prediction on Amazon stock
detail:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy makes a strong prediction on Amazon stock
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 7:03 AM CDT 6 min read
AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Amazon just gave Wall Street a quarter it didn't love and a prediction it can't ignore.

Shares slid after the company's third-quarter report, but CEO Andy Jassy used the moment to float a goal no company has ever reached.

"There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years," Jassy said in the earnings release.

It's a bold claim, and it puts the spotlight back on what the company's giant spending spree is actually buying.

Amazon's solid quarter still disappointed

On paper, the results looked healthy. Amazon's net sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion, and operating income jumped to $28.1 billion from $17.4 billion a year earlier, good for a 13.9% operating margin that the company called its highest ever, according to Amazon.

Moving Prime Day into the second quarter cut about four percentage points off third-quarter growth.

Also read: Billionaire Bill Ackman doubles down on these stocks in Q2

Investors focused on the misses instead. Revenue came in just shy of the roughly $202.3 billion analysts expected, and earnings of $1.89 a share fell short of the $1.96 forecast. The stock fell about 6% in overnight trading on Oct. 29, even though advertising revenue reached $19.6 billion.

The bigger worry was cash. Amazon's free cash flow over the past 12 months swung to an outflow of $42.4 billion, compared with a $14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, and the company blamed heavier spending on AI infrastructure, Amazon reported.

It still expects about $220 billion in cash capital spending this year. For the fourth quarter, Amazon guided for net sales of $240 billion to $247 billion and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

The capex number has been climbing all year. Amazon first planned about $200 billion in 2026 capital spending back in February, well above what Wall Street expected, and the stock fell more than 10% on the news. Investors have been asking ever since when all that spending will pay off.

The road to $1 trillion in e-commerce

Jassy's two candidates are Amazon's online stores and its cloud unit, Amazon Web Services. Retail is the much bigger of the two today, and it has the shorter path.

Amazon's North America and International segments, which make up the e-commerce business, brought in $638.3 billion over the past four quarters, and that business has been growing at a low-teens rate in recent years, according to The Motley Fool. At a 10% annual growth rate, that business would top $1 trillion in under five years.

Trading disclosure
Amazon Is 16% Off Its High After a Record Quarter: Take Profits, or Buy More? ©VIktoryia Vinnikava from Viktoryia Vinnikava's Images and AndreyPopov from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Amazon's third-quarter revenue rose 12% to $201.9 billion and AWS grew 39% to $46.0 billion, but EPS of $1.89 missed the $1.96 estimate.

Capex hit $77.3 billion in the quarter against a $58.7 billion consensus, and trailing free cash flow swung to negative $42.4 billion.

Fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $240 billion to $247 billion trails consensus at the midpoint, and Amazon plans to spend meaningfully more on capex in 2027.

The expected February 4 report needs to show AWS growth holding near 40% and a credible path back to positive free cash flow.

Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) just printed the highest operating margin in its history. The stock slipped anyway, closing Friday at $240, down 1.4% and 16% below its 52-week high of $287.

Blame the cash flow statement. Amazon spent $77.3 billion on capex in the third quarter, and trailing free cash flow fell to negative $42.4 billion.

A big share of that spending lands at Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ), which plans to deploy 2 million more of its GPUs across AWS in 2027 and 2028. Amazon also has company in the red. Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) reported the first negative free cash flow quarter of its public life a week earlier, at negative $2.12 billion.

So AWS growth no longer settles the debate. Investors want to know when all this spending turns back into cash.

A record margin with a miss attached

Revenue rose 12% to $201.9 billion, just under the $202.3 billion consensus. EPS of $1.89 missed the $1.96 estimate, and net income fell 2% because the year-ago quarter included a $9.5 billion pre-tax gain on Amazon's Anthropic stake.

Higher up the income statement, the quarter was excellent:

Operating income jumped 61% to $28.1 billion, a record 13.9% margin.

AWS revenue grew 39% to $46.0 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years.

The AWS backlog reached $496 billion.

Guidance was softer. Amazon sees fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, and the $243.5 billion midpoint sits below the $244.5 billion consensus. Its operating income range of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion still compares well with $25.0 billion a year earlier.

Profitability has stepped up quickly…
